A release happens in two steps. First we upload every new asset under a versioned name, so it never overwrites an existing file. Then we switch the manifest so it points to those new names.

The upload comes before the switch so the manifest never points at a file that doesn't exist yet. Once the manifest changes, browsers start requesting the new names immediately. If those files were still uploading, users would get 404s and broken pages. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest is already live when the switch happens.

We keep the old assets because some browsers already fetched the previous manifest and will keep requesting the files it lists, such as a tab that was open during the release. If we deleted those files, those users would hit missing scripts and styles partway through their session. Versioned names let both sets of files exist side by side, so old and new manifests each resolve to a complete, consistent set of assets.

Each release uploads every new asset under a new versioned name and then switches the manifest to point at those names. The order and the cleanup policy both protect users who load the site during or after the change.

The upload comes first because the manifest is what sends browsers to assets. If we switched the manifest first, a browser could fetch it and request a versioned file that hasn't been uploaded yet, and that request would fail. Uploading first means every name the new manifest mentions already exists when a browser first sees it. The switch then works as a single cutover from fully available old assets to fully available new ones.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already have the previous one. Those browsers will keep requesting the old versioned names. If we deleted those files, their pages would break partway through. Because each release uses new names, the old files never conflict with the new ones, so keeping them serves those browsers at no risk to the new release.

A release happens in two steps: first we upload every new asset under a versioned name (for example `app.3f9c2a.js`), and only then do we switch the manifest so it points to those new names.

The upload comes first because the manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it before the files were in place, any browser that fetched the new manifest in that gap would request assets that don't exist yet and get a broken page. Uploading first means every name the new manifest references is already servable when the manifest goes live, so the switch itself is the single moment the release takes effect.

We keep the old assets because browsers that loaded the previous manifest will keep requesting the old versioned names, for example when they lazy-load a chunk or an image later in the session. If we deleted those files at release time, those users would hit missing assets mid-session. Leaving them up lets the old manifest and the new one both work at once, so users move to the new version on their next manifest fetch without anything breaking in between. Versioned names make this safe, because the old and new files never overwrite each other.

When we release, we first upload every new asset under a versioned name, such as `app.3f9c2.js`, and only then switch the manifest to point at those new names. Old assets stay where they are.

**Why the upload comes first:** the manifest switch is the moment browsers start asking for the new files. If we switched first, any browser that fetched the new manifest before the uploads finished would request files that don't exist yet. That means broken pages, missing styles, or failed scripts. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves by the time anyone can see it, so the switch is effectively atomic.

**Why we keep the old assets:** a browser that loaded the previous manifest will keep requesting the asset names it lists, for example when it lazy-loads a chunk or navigates within an already-open page. If we deleted those files at release, those users would get 404s mid-session. Because versioned names never collide, the old and new sets can sit side by side. Each browser gets a consistent set of files matching the manifest it actually has.
